title: Altoids Project | Lu’s blog
content:
Altoids Project
Oct 31, 2026
My 12-year-old son and I spent about two months on, what we call, the Altoids project. Here is the final product (video):
It all started when I took him to MIT Swapfest for the first time. We saw an assembled robot from a couple’s booth; later we learned that it was from a kit. It was built by their daughter many years ago. After realizing I had come with my son, they gave us the robot for free. We also picked up a used ThinkPad laptop at a very reasonable price, which we used for the project.
As any curious mind would, we disassembled the robot. Noticing that we were missing the control, we wanted to see which parts we could reuse. We took the 128x64 display off. But we couldn’t find the pinout for the display. We tried using AI, but it hallucinated so badly that it gave us a 20-pin pinout when the display only has 10 pins.
After hours of searching around, we found the exact schematic posted on Arduino’s forum by a stranger on the Internet. God bless him. With the pinout, we finally made the display show something. We ran the Space Trash game from the U8g2 library. Let’s call this v1.
I had just watched a YouTube video where someone built a tiny computer and fit everything inside an Altoids tin (video). Inspired by the YouTube video, we grabbed a random tin found in the house and moved the project to the workbench.
To reduce the form factor, we switched to an Arduino Nano, and ordered LiPo batteries and PowerBoost for power supply. Everything needed to fit in the tin. My son did all the CAD and 3D printing. Here is what v2 looked like. The lid did not close. It felt like playing 3D chess to fit everything in.
We ordered solderable breadboards to avoid the messy wires. It was looking promising. We also bought a real tin of Altoids from a grocery store, since the Altoids tin is actually a little taller than the one we were using earlier. This is what v3 looked like. The lid did not close, but we were getting closer.
The display was connected to a tiny solderable breadboard. We wanted to remove it and connect the wires to the display directly. But we had a really hard time with desoldering. We accidentally pulled one copper pad off the display, making it unusable. We might be possible to salvage it, but we just ordered a new display from Adafruit instead.
At this point, I wanted to avoid desoldering as much as possible. So we got those tiny hooks for testing the display (video). This is when we realized the new display does not default to SPI mode. We did not want to make more changes to the wiring, so we still had to desolder two jumpers.
I suspected our soldering iron was heating unevenly. We ordered a new soldering iron and it made all the difference. With the new iron, we made rapid progress. We hot-glued the display onto the lid. Everything worked for the first time. This is what v4 looked like. The lid did close with some struggle.
Two wires connecting the microcontroller and the display broke the next day. We did many hacks, one of which is to extend the wires by soldering two wires together. It did not work well, obviously. We got some ultra-fine (30 AWG) wires to replace them. At this point, my son did most of the desoldering and soldering work. He actually connected one wire incorrectly, so it did not work at first. It is a good debugging and learning experience.
As a final touch, we got tiny 1x1-inch ziploc bags and put two actual Altoids in the tin. And here we have the final product, after five iterations. None of the components used in the first iteration survived.

title: Early Electric Vehicles Were Designed With Women in Mind - IEEE Spectrum
content:
At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.
For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.
Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.
Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.
In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.MISCI—MUSEUM OF INNOVATION AND SCIENCE
A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.
Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier?
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. BETTMANN/GETTY IMAGES
Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.
The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.
A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric Cars
I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.
This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.HERITAGE MUSEUMS & GARDENS
According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.
Thomas Edison Designed a Bad Battery
Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.
While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).
Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.SARAH THORNINGTON/HERITAGE MUSEUMS & GARDENS
Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.
When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.
Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. MISCI—MUSEUM OF INNOVATION AND SCIENCE
Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)
Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.
Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.
Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.
An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.
References
For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.
Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

title: It's the memory latency, stupid · Pivot blog
content:
← All posts
It's the memory latency, stupid
Making GROUP BY faster by doing more (CPU!) work
October 28, 2026 · Maor Kern
DISCLAIMER
no LLMs were harmed (or for that matter used) in the writing of this blog post
When you see your databases CPU at 100%, what is it actually doing? We like to act as though CPUs run code linearly for simplicity's sake, but in truth CPUs are incredibly complex beasts; they can potentially do many instructions at once, or sometimes none at all (despite our console showing 100%). Because CPUs can do so many things, one CPU at 100% may be doing much less than another at 100%. A CPU is considered "idle" only if no task (Linux task) needs CPU time; this does not mean the CPU itself is being fully saturated. So why would a CPU not be fully utilized, even if it appears to be at 100%?
The answer is usually memory.
Memory accesses are orders of magnitude slower than internal CPU operations. To give a good picture of how much so, a modern CPU might be able to process somewhere in the realm of 4-8 instructions per nanosecond. A memory access to RAM can take somewhere in the realm of 50-100ns. To ease your mathing, that means a modern CPU can do around 400-800 instructions for every one memory access from RAM.
CPU
CPU core
4–8 instr / ns
L1 cache
~1 ns
~64 KB · ~4–8 instructions per access
L2 cache
~3–4 ns
~1 MB · ~15–30 instructions per access
L3 cache
~10–15 ns
up to a few hundred MB · ~50–100 instructions per access
DRAM
~50–100 ns
GBs · ~400–800 instructions per access
Given this, CPUs are built from the ground up to work their way around this. The most obvious way this is dealt with is CPU caches. CPU caches keep memory closer to the CPU than RAM, literally baked into the CPU chip. The closest cache (the L1 cache) takes around 1ns per memory operation- that's 50-100x faster than RAM! The "problem" here of course is that the CPU caches are fairly small; the L1 cache for a modern CPU is probably around ~64KB, while the farther caches max out at a few hundred MB for top end processors. A good database tries manipulating data in small "chunks" to take full advantage of caches, and you'll often hear cache utilization as being one of the top concerns of performance engineering.
Let's look at GROUP BY aggregations to get a better grip on cache utilization. In GROUP BY, we're looking to take a dataset, group it by a certain column (or more), and perform certain aggregations (for example, count, or sum on another column). The "naive" method might be to open a HashTable keyed by the group key that grows ever larger. For every new row, you would check if that key exists- if it does, go to it's corresponding aggregation and update the result. Simple, right? The problem is that if you have millions of unique groups, you're not utilizing your cache at all! Nearly every HashTable access will be a "cold" hit that goes to RAM. This means that although your CPU may /look/ like it's 100% utilized, in truth it'll constantly be waiting for cold memory accesses.
To demonstrate this, we'll take our state-of-the-art Pivot engine and ravage it! We'll remove all our complex logic and replace it with simplicity:
fn consume(
    &mut self,
    batch: RecordBatch,
    _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>,
) -> unary::Result<()> {
    let group_keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>();
    for &key in group_keys.values() {
        // If the Group Key doesn't exist- set it to 0
        // Afterwards, add 1 to the group- this will give us a count(*) GROUP BY key_column
        *self.counts.entry(key).or_insert(0) += 1;
    }
}
We'll then run a simple query SELECT count(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID on the "hits" dataset ClickBench provides (99m rows). This query will give us a count per UserID, meaning we'll have an entry in our HashMap per UserID- I'll give a spoiler here that there are ~17m unique UserID.
Our performance checks will be on a bare metal server from our good friends over at CherryServers (AMD EPYC 9124 Genoa, 16 cores, 128 GB DDR5). We unfortunately can't use a common AWS/GCP machine because we want access to counters that aren't exposed there for security reasons (for example, we want to see how much memory is passing from DRAM controller to us). We'll confine ourselves to a single core, since this naive group by can't run on many cores.
To run it:
cat > config.yaml <<'EOF'
server:
  bind: 127.0.0.1:5440
workers: 1
datastores:
  default:
    kind: pivotlake
    location: ./data
    default: true
users:
  pivot:
    auth:
      method: trust
EOF
taskset -c 3 pivot server --config config.yaml &
taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
This takes... a whopping 3.9 seconds. Is that good? Is that bad? Everything in this world is relative, or so they say. If we run the query again (without restarting the server), it takes 3.6s. The second run is the one we're more interested in- there's no disk involved as everything is already sitting in our page-cache.
You'll notice we did taskset -c. This pins the process to a given CPU; this will allow us to run perf stat on that CPU and see what's going on internally. We'll measure two metric groups- percentage of CPU slots stalling because of memory (and not doing anything in the meanwhile), and percentage of CPU slots actually retiring a micro-op:
sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
and we get back this
Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        8364109137      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     50.1 %  backend_bound_memory
       38233214040      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        8977647849      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       11861387798      ls_not_halted_cyc
       11431618219      ex_ret_ops                       #     16.1 %  retiring
       11858248045      ls_not_halted_cyc

       4.030148989 seconds time elapsed
This tells us that 50.1% of the time, the CPU couldn't do anything because it was stalling on memory! And only 16.1% of the time the CPU was actually retiring (aka doing) operations.
Another interesting stat to get is how many of our CPU memory loads are coming from DRAM (and not from caches):
sudo perf stat -C 3   -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
And the result:
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          76190837      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.996301634 seconds time elapsed
Every load is 64 bytes (the minimum amount you can bring, a cache line), so we can multiply by 64 to see we pulled 4.5GB during this query from DRAM on CPU loads (this is without any prefetching).
Let's now try to improve our algorithm to take advantage of the CPU caches. To do this, we'll use a method called radix partitioning. The idea is to split the merge into two distinct phases:
Phase 1: In this phase, we're simply going to separate the keys into 4096 different partitions (simply a Vec of SlabVecs- a SlabVec is a data structure similar to a Vec that is above memory that is already paged in. We don't use Vecs for raw memory in Pivot because it creates a lot of variance; not something for this blog post!). The partition will be decided by hashing the key and taking it's top 12 bits (2**12=4096).
fn consume(
    &mut self,
    batch: RecordBatch,
    _sender: &mut dyn Sender<RecordBatch>,
) -> unary::Result<()> {
    let keys = batch.column(self.key_column).as_primitive::<Int64Type>();
    for &key in keys.values() {
        let hash = self.hasher.hash_one(key);
        // Since we want top 12 bits, we shift the hash (a u64) 52 bits to the right
        let partition = (hash >> 52) as usize;
        self.partitions[partition].push(&mut self.allocator, (hash, key));
    }
    Ok(())
}
UserID hash(UserID)

→

Phase 2: When all data has come through, go partition by partition, each time creating a HashMap, aggregating the partition into it, and then outputting it. This phase is very similar to our original algorithm, but we're going to use the hash from phase 1.
fn into_outputter(self) -> unary::Result<Option<Self::Outputter>> {
    let mut groups = Vec::new();
    for rows in &self.partitions {
        let mut table: HashTable<(u64, i64, u64)> = HashTable::new();   // (hash, key, count)
        rows.for_each(|(hash, key)| {
            match table.entry(hash, |group| group.1 == key, |group| group.0) {
                Entry::Occupied(mut group) => group.get_mut().2 += 1,
                Entry::Vacant(slot) => { slot.insert((hash, key, 1)); }
            }
        });
        groups.extend(table.into_iter().map(|(_, key, count)| (key, count)));
    }
    Ok(Some(Outputter::new(groups)))
}
PARTITIONS, ONE AT A TIME

At first glance, this solution may seem rather odd. We're doing more operations here, not less! Every row, in both solutions, is hashed and sent into a HashMap. But in this solution, we're first pushing rows into seemingly meaningless vecs.
The key here (no pun intended) is to understand why we've done this; it's to make the aggregating HashMaps smaller. By dividing our group by into 4096 pieces, we've made our working HashMaps much likelier to fit into our CPU caches. Every time we do a lookup on our HashMap, our CPU is more likely to find the relevant memory sitting in it's caches, which saves a big chunk of time. But why trust me? Let's run it!
taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c '\timing on' -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
And... Boom! 3.3 seconds, and then on second run 2.7 seconds! We've definitely made an improvement. But to really drive this point home, let's run perf again:
sudo perf stat -C 3 -M backend_bound_memory,retiring -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
And our results:
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

        3790955223      ex_no_retire.load_not_complete   #     23.5 %  backend_bound_memory
       20376118172      de_no_dispatch_per_slot.backend_stalls
        5442424751      ex_no_retire.not_complete
       10083617764      ls_not_halted_cyc
       19350459182      ex_ret_ops                       #     32.2 %  retiring
       10023435553      ls_not_halted_cyc

       3.575992317 seconds time elapsed
Now we can see the picture has completely changed- 23.5% of the time is spent on waiting for memory (as opposed to 50% before), 32% for actually retiring operations. You may notice we're actually doing more work, not less- in this run, we did 19350459182 operations (the ex_ret_ops counter), whereas before the database did 11431618219 operations. This is worth it though, because as we said before- if we can translate cold DRAM accesses into CPU instructions, it's nearly always a good trade to make. In this case, we went down from 8364109137 CPU slots stalled because of memory to 3790955223.
To complete the picture and really see we're pulling less memory from the DRAM, let's again check how many our memory loads come from DRAM:
sudo perf stat -C 3   -e ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near   -- taskset -c 7 psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5440 -U pivot -c "SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*), UserID FROM hits GROUP BY UserID)"
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          25688280      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       3.009547012 seconds time elapsed
Whoo! That means that on demand we pulled 1.5GB from DRAM, instead of 4.5GB in the naive version.
That, of course, isn't the limit of how much we can utilize our CPU cache for GROUP BYs. And utilizing our CPU cache isn't the only way we can "hide" DRAM latency; another trick is prefetching memory to our cache before we need it, and yet another trick is creating algorithms that allow maximization of memory throughput- but that's not for this blog! We'll go into that in our next blog where we look at our /seemingly very weird/ implementation of JOIN probing.
For now, without explaining too much, I'll leave you with Pivot's speed for this query on a single core:
Time: 1848.353 ms (00:01.848)
and the amount of RAM we bring:
 Performance counter stats for 'CPU(s) 3':

          14917958      ls_dmnd_fills_from_sys.dram_io_near

       2.182674864 seconds time elapsed
Which comes out to 954 MB.
Of course, Pivot knows to run in parallel on our 16 cores (where there are many other interesting cases), in which case it comes out to:
Time: 171.773 ms
nice :)
Try out Pivot if you want to have super speeds above parquets (OSS fun!), see you next time.

title: Zinc creep in the cable spelter sockets brought down the 57 year old Arecibo telescope in 2020, a failure sequence that began with Hurricane Maria three years earlier and the first documented case of long term zinc creep in over a century of use. - Make Tech Easier
content:
The Arecibo telescope in Puerto Rico before its collapse. Photo: Clembore Memotech, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
+ CURIOSITIES & REAL-WORLD STORIES
+ CURIOSITIES
Zinc creep in the cable spelter sockets brought down the 57 year old Arecibo telescope in 2020, a failure sequence that began with Hurricane Maria three years earlier and the first documented case of long term zinc creep in over a century of use.
By Make Tech Easier Editorial
Staff byline
Published Oct 30, 2026
SHARE
Copy link
X
Email
Long-term zinc creep in the cable spelter sockets was the root cause of the 2020 collapse of the National Science Foundation’s 57-year-old telescope at the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico, according to a report from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, which also draws lessons learned for other unique, critical science facilities.
The failure sequence began with Hurricane Maria, over three years before the collapse, the report says.
The telescope’s main platform hung over the 305-metre reflector dish on a set of cables. Each cable ended in a socket filled with zinc, and the zinc held the cable in place. The report says the zinc gradually lost its hold on the cables and allowed several of them to pull out. The platform then fell into the reflector.
A failure mode with no documented precedent
Zinc-filled sockets of this kind have been in use for more than a century, the report notes. It calls the Arecibo failure “the first documented case of long-term zinc-induced creep failure despite a long history of usage over a century”. Before the hurricane, indications of cable pullout were minimal.
After the hurricane, visual inspections showed large and progressive cable pullouts, which the report says should have prompted remedial action. Safety factor calculations made after the first cable failure did not recognise the accelerated time-dependent materials failure process that governed the eventual zinc pullout.
EDITORS’ RECOMMENDATIONS
From the cockpit of an F-22, a pilot acted as an airborne quarterback for a YFQ-44A Fury in October, handing it tactical directives instead of stick-and-rudder commands; Anduril says it was a first for the Raptor and the pre-production drone.
A cliff on Uranus’s moon Miranda is about six miles high, and because gravity there is less than 1% of Earth’s, anyone who stepped off the top would fall for around eight minutes and reach the bottom at roughly highway speed
ASTRONAUTIX
Xbox Game Pass caps cloud streaming in November 2026 at 15 hours a month on Ultimate, 10 on Premium and 5 on Essential, with 10 more hours costing $3.99.
The electroplasticity hypothesis
The report offers one possible explanation for why the creep accelerated.
Long-term low-current electroplasticity, induced by the electromagnetic waves from the Arecibo telescope itself, may have sped up the zinc creep, it says. The report recommends that NSF offer the remaining socket and cable sections for study by the research community.
More broadly, the report says building and operating cutting-edge, custom-designed research facilities presents unique challenges, where prior designs and experience may not be a reliable guide and unprecedented modes of failure can never be fully anticipated.
EDITORS’ RECOMMENDATIONS
Akihiko Kondo's unofficial 2018 wedding to the virtual singer Hatsune Miku, a hologram on his shelf, cost about 2 million yen. Can a partner who can never say no be one?
PHILOSOPHY BASICS

PHILOSOPHY BASICS

Careful monitoring should be increased as facilities age, to detect deterioration and potential novel failure modes, to the extent that is reasonable, it says.
The report also says NSF should make explicit funding provisions for detailed, ongoing condition maintenance and monitoring. NSF maintained research operations at Arecibo for its National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center.
The committee that wrote the report reviewed forensic investigations commissioned by the University of Central Florida and NSF, gathered information from Arecibo Observatory employees, studied relevant research, consulted other experts, and examined structural analyses, engineering plans, inspection reports, photographs and repair proposals.
The full report, a consensus study report published in 2024, is titled Failure Analysis of the Arecibo Observatory 305-Meter Telescope Collapse. The National Academies announced its release in a media advisory last updated on October 25, 2024.
It also contains recommendations on operations and maintenance manuals, inspection regimes and independent audits.

title: Edgar Allan Poe is the most influential American writer. It’s time to admit it.
content:
BOOKS
Edgar Allan Poe, Quintessential American Writer
It’s time to acknowledge just how influential he was.
BY LAURA MILLER
FOLLOW LAURA MILLER
OCT 25, 20265:40 AM
Sepia Times/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
COMMENT
COPY LINK
GIFT STORY
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
Who is the quintessential American writer? Whenever anyone starts kicking around that question, some predictable names turn up: Mark Twain, Herman Melville, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway, Toni Morrison. Rarely, though, does anyone mention Edgar Allan Poe, even though Poe is arguably the most influential American writer of all. In fact, after poking around online, I found just one site that listed Poe as No. 1 in the “Top 10 American Writers,” an MIT-affiliated outfit called Pantheon.world that claims to use “biographical data to expose patterns of human collective memory” via a “slow and painful process.” Whatever that means, Pantheon draws from international sources, and without a doubt, Poe is more highly revered abroad than in his own homeland.
Emily Ogden’s Darkness Becomes Bright: On the Brief Life and Immortal Art of Edgar Allan Poe is a step toward correcting that. This slim, sinuous collection of essays on Poe’s influence, published earlier this fall, braids together strands of memoir, biography, and literary criticism to make a case for Poe as a writer whose “fundamental theme is the human cry issuing from desperate extremity,” and whose global impact has been formidable. A professor of English at the University of Virginia (a school Poe himself attended for one term back in 1826), Ogden writes that, “in the space of Poe’s works, some of us have been able to tolerate ourselves as we actually are: limited, cruel, perverse, and mortal, but, for all that, still glittering with a heavenly light.” To illustrate this, she explores what three non-American writers—the Argentinian novelist Julio Cortázar, the psychoanalyst Marie Bonaparte, and the French poet Charles Baudelaire—found revelatory and essential in Poe’s writing.
It’s easy to see, though, why Poe doesn’t fit within many Americans’ notion of our literature. With the exception of a short, early, and minor work, The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, he wrote no novels, the most exalted literary form during the 20th century, when the nation’s literary culture reached its maturity. Poe’s most famous tales and poetry make no effort to depict American life or social issues, and tend to take place in fantastical and vaguely European settings: moldering manor houses or the dungeons of the Spanish Inquisition. In fact, the settings of most of Poe’s stories feel detached from any real-world locations. They are the stuff of dreams, or rather, nightmares.
Join Slate Plus to keep reading: “One Literary Giant Is Rarely Associated With His Homeland. Make No Mistake: He’s the Most Influential American Writer of All.”
Unlock unlimited reading, bonus podcast episodes, ad-free listening, every Slate Game, and more. Try 3 months for just $5 per month.
Join Slate Plus
Already a member?
Sign in here.
Poe’s work, furthermore, seems in deliberate, even flagrant, contrast with what were once regarded as the great themes of American literature: the freedom of self-reinvention promised by a new society and its frontier, exploration, rugged individualism, and the struggle to conquer nature. Where other writers saw the American landscape as offering room to prove oneself and forge a destiny unfettered by the past, Poe’s tales and poems are claustrophobic and fatalistic. Tombs, prisons, catacombs, and walled-up alcoves abound in his fiction. Even when his characters aren’t physically confined, they are trapped by some inescapable doom: madness, guilt, grief, or the plague that stalks the aristocratic revelers in “The Masque of the Red Death.” Instead of optimistic and outgoing—the European stereotype of Americans—they are morbid and withdrawn. Instead of persevering against all odds, they despair.
Darkness Becomes Bright: On the Brief Life and Immortal Art of Edgar Allan Poe
By Emily Ogden. Viking.

title: Jepsen: ParticleDB 1.1.4
content:
1 Background
Modern applications often spread state across a variety of systems: databases, caches, queues, data warehouses, search indices, and so on. Coordinating these systems is challenging: caches are often stale, the analytics platform might lag days behind the primary database, the search index might lose data, and transactional updates across disparate systems remains an open research problem.
ParticleDB1 aims to unify these workloads in a single engine with a special focus on AI agents and applications. It offers transactional SQL, a key-value store, vector search, live analytics, and user-defined functions called Particles.2 To integrate with existing systems, clients can connect through a variety of interfaces, including the Postgres and Redis protocols, as well as its own gRPC and HTTP2 APIs. Written from the ground up in Rust, ParticleDB claims to be orders of magnitude faster than Postgres while preserving the same safety characteristics.
ParticleDB was built by Orkes to support their workflow orchestration platform, Conductor. Conductor was initially built to store data in Redis and Postgres, but to improve performance, Orkes opted to write their own database. ParticleDB 1.0.0 offered a limited feature set specifically for Conductor’s queries, and was deployed as the backing database for some of their Conductor clusters. A few Orkes customers followed suit. In preparation for a broader release, Orkes undertook a major refactoring of ParticleDB, adding a custom wire protocol, more datatypes, additional OLAP queries, and more. While Orkes and their customers continued to run 1.0.0, they soft launched the refactored versions on particledb.ai. Orkes engaged Jepsen to test these versions of ParticleDB, beginning with 1.1.4.
While ParticleDB could run as a single node, it also offered a replicated cluster using the Raft consensus protocol. This replication feature was available only in enterprise cloud deployments. The builds Orkes provided did not support replication, so this report covers only single-node behavior.
1.1 Safety
ParticleDB’s home page advertised that ParticleDB was “formally proven” with a TLA+ proof. However, during our collaboration no TLA+ specification was available. It is unclear what properties might be proven, or whether they described ParticleDB as built.
ParticleDB offered three tactics for syncing its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). The sync mode called fsync on each commit, groupsync batched multiple transactions into a single fsync, and nosync skipped fsync altogether. The Transaction Engine documentation described sync as offering “stronger durability” than groupsync. On the other hand, particledb start --help said the groupsync mode ensured that “COMMIT waits for flush”, and Orkes’ internal operator guide concurred: groupsync offered the “same durability as sync”.
ParticleDB’s home page proudly claimed “Full ACID. 159K TPS.” However, the text immediately below this said “snapshot isolation”, which is not fully isolated.
Most SQL databases use the SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL statement to control the concurrent semantics of a transaction. However, ParticleDB ignored or rejected these statements. In some cases it instructed users to choose READ COMMITTED, a relatively weak isolation level. In other cases it accepted requests for different isolation levels, and silently ignored them (despite documentation to the contrary).
Instead, transaction isolation was governed by the --txn-mode setting passed at startup. The transaction engine documentation described four modes:
Mode Behavior When to use
fast No locks; commit-on-write Bulk loads, single-writer benchmarks
occ Overlay + commit-time OCC validation (default) General OLTP — safe under concurrency
zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC; single-partition txns skip cross-partition coordination High-throughput OLTP on partition-affine workloads (TPC-C, key-value)
table-2pl Exclusive table locks at first touch Strictest serialization, simple semantics
This table was difficult to interpret. While the best practices documentation warned that users should “pick --txn-mode deliberately”, since “it changes correctness and throughput characteristics more than SQL text does”, the documentation did not explain what these modes actually guaranteed. The fast mode was clearly intended for weaker isolation, but was that Read Atomic, Read Uncommitted, or something else? The occ mode was similarly unclear. “Commit-time OCC validation” could describe a broad spectrum of consistency models from Read Uncommitted to Strong Serializable, but “safe under concurrency” suggests it might be Serializable. The zero-copy-occ mode described a performance optimization which could be as safe as occ, but it was not described as “safe under concurrency”—raising the question: in what ways was it unsafe? Finally, if table-2pl offered the “strictest serialization”, was occ some weaker isolation level?
The CLI reference page contained another table which described occ and table-2pl as “Jepsen-safe”, whereas fast was not “Jepsen-safe”, but did not explain their safety properties. Since Jepsen evaluates safety with respect to documentation and marketing claims, it is not clear how to interpret these terms.3
Running particledb start --help provided the following table:
Mode Description
fast No locks, maximum OLTP throughput (unsafe under concurrency)
occ Table locks + commit-time validation (safe for most OLTP)
row-2pl Alias for occ
zero-copy-occ Partition-pinned OCC (highest throughput safe mode)
table-2pl Exclusive table locks, full serialization (strictest)
serializable Alias for table-2pl
serializable-ssi Adaptive SSI (Cahill 2008), PL-3 with optimistic semantics (v1 scaffolding — see SSI_ADAPTIVE_DESIGN.md)
The point of Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) is generally to avoid taking locks, so the mention of table locks and a row-2pl4 alias was surprising. Moreover, “safe for most OLTP” undermines the claim that occ was “safe under concurrency”; it suggests there are some OLTP workloads which are unsafe!
Orkes explained that this documentation was wrong: occ was actually optimistic, and the row-2pl alias was to preserve compatibility with an earlier two-phase locking mechanism. They also provided an unpublished operator guide with detailed descriptions of the various transaction modes. This document was difficult to interpret, but did specify the following consistency models:
Mode Consistency Model
fast Unknown
occ-v3 (a.k.a. occ, occ-v2, row-2pl) Snapshot Isolation
zero-copy-occ (a.k.a. zocc) Snapshot Isolation
serializable-ssi (a.k.a. ssi) Serializable
table-2pl (a.k.a. serializable) Strong Serializable
Sources disagreed about the default transaction and WAL sync modes, but in general, occ-v3 and groupsync appeared to be the default.
2 Test Design
We wrote a test suite for ParticleDB using the Jepsen testing library. We ran ParticleDB versions 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.11.rc-22 on individual Debian 13 nodes, both in containers and EC2 VMs. Our test harness could simulate process crashes by killing ParticleDB, simulate the loss of un-fsynced writes using LazyFS, and truncate or corrupt disk files. We ran ParticleDB using each transaction mode and all three WAL sync modes.
We first tried ParticleDB’s official Java SDK. While the documentation indicated that the library was available as a Maven dependency, neither the JAR nor source code were actually available. Instead, we began with the official Postgres JDBC client, version 42.7.11, and later added support for the ParticleDB Java SDK, versions 1.0.0 through 1.0.2.
2.1 Workloads
We used several Jepsen workloads from other SQL databases, and designed new ones specifically for ParticleDB.
The rw workload performed randomly generated transactions involving reads and writes of integer values identified by unique integer keys. We stored each value in a single row and accessed them both via primary and unindexed secondary keys. Keys and values were encoded as a variety of datatypes, including integers, decimals, and strings. We assumed that writes followed reads within each transaction, and that individual keys were sequentially consistent, and used these assumptions to infer constraints on the version orders and transaction dependency graphs. Jepsen’s transactional checker, Elle, then searched for cycles in that dependency graph, as well as a variety of non-cyclic phenomena like G1a (Aborted Read).
The append workload also performed randomly generated transactions over rows identified by unique integer keys, but the values were lists of integers. Transactions could read one of these lists by key, or append a unique integer to a list by key. We encoded each list as a comma-separated text field, and used SQL concat to append to them. Rows could be selected via primary key or unindexed secondary key, or via a join to an indirection table. From there, we used Elle to infer version orders and dependency graphs, and searched for a variety of cyclic and non-cyclic phenomena.
When these workloads revealed consistency violations within a single transaction, we designed an internal workload to stress internal consistency. This workload performed a series of randomly generated transactions involving INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT statements over a simple key-value table, and verified that within each individual transaction, reads observed prior writes.
To investigate tantalizing anomalies in the internal workload, we designed the compare workload. This workload used Clojure’s test.check generative testing library to produce random tables and simple SQL statements over them, then executed those statements against both ParticleDB and PostgreSQL. If ParticleDB’s behavior was not equivalent to PostgreSQL’s, the compare workload would search for a simpler sequence of statements that could reproduce the same divergence. Although our SQL generator was relatively simple—just a few basic datatypes, literals, arithmetic, comparisons, boolean logic, transactions, and some simple LIMIT, OFFSET, and ORDER BY clauses—it proved remarkably fruitful.
Drawing on these successes, we devised a hybrid internal-sim workload to search for violations of internal consistency in more complex transactions. This workload generated a random set of tables, then concurrently executed random transactions over them. It then checked each transaction independently to ensure that each of its statements observed results consistent with those preceding. For example, if a transaction executed DELETE ... WHERE 2 < c, then observed a row with c = 3, we could prove that transaction was not internally consistent.
3 Results
We found 96 issues with ParticleDB, which we present in several categories below. All but three of these issues occurred in healthy, single-node instances of ParticleDB. Busy readers may wish to jump to the Discussion section, which summarizes our findings.
Availability and Performance
Broken Features
Predicates
Constraints
Joins
Zombies
State Corruption
Transactions and Concurrency
With Faults
Additional results are presented in Appendix A:
Type Safety and Syntax
Arithmetic
Strings
3.1 Availability and Performance
Under normal operation, ParticleDB was slow, deadlocked, and crashed without warning.
3.1.1 Abysmal Performance With table-2pl (#62)
In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, --txn-mode table-2pl was so slow as to be essentially unusable. While some transactions might complete in a few milliseconds, most took 10, 20, or even 30 seconds, then failed.
For example, take this test run with a single node running 1.1.18.4, transaction mode table-2pl, and WAL mode groupsync. With ten concurrent clients, most transactions blocked for tens of seconds before throwing could not serialize access due to concurrent update, or an IO error.
High latencies (#62) appeared improved by 1.1.18.6, which could execute transactions with sub-100 millisecond latencies for at least a few seconds.
3.1.2 Mystery Crash (#81)
While 1.1.18.6 improved latencies, it also crashed frequently. Crashes occurred spontaneously with various transaction modes, WAL modes, and client interfaces; there was no obvious cause. Nodes would run for a few hundred to a few thousand seconds before exiting. No error messages were printed. These crashes (#81) no longer appeared in 1.1.18.11.rc-18.
3.1.3 Deadlock After Two Transactions (#27)
In ParticleDB 1.1.18.8, submitting as few as two concurrent transactions to a healthy, single-node deployment could cause it to deadlock. This occurred both using the Postgres and ParticleDB interfaces. The node would log an error message like [DEADLOCK] 1 cycles detected at SystemTime ..., and an empty backtrace. In some cases new clients could attach and perform transactions; in others, new clients would also hang indefinitely. This may reflect multiple deadlock bugs.
With the append workload, version 1.1.18.9 generally could not run for more than 45 seconds without locking up. Version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 could reliably run for two minutes without lockups, and we declared the issue (#27) resolved.
3.1.4 Deadlock With table-2pl (#71)
While version 1.1.18.11.rc-1 fixed the most frequent deadlocks, we continued to find deadlocks through 1.1.18.11.rc-6 when running with table-2pl. An otherwise healthy ParticleDB node would execute transactions for about 30 seconds, then get stuck forever. The node would log a similar deadlock error message to #27, and all requests with the ParticleDB client would throw PDB JDBC: null after a 100 second default timeout. These deadlocks (#71) appeared resolved by 1.1.18.11.rc-7.
3.2 Broken Features
Orkes’ public documentation claimed broad support for Postgres features, and the internal operator guide concurred:
The engine speaks PostgreSQL v3 wire protocol natively — anything that speaks pgjdbc / libpq / psycopg2 / pq connects unchanged. BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, prepared statements, parameterised queries, and extended-query pipelining all work as expected.
These claims were somewhat optimistic. ParticleDB was missing support for a wide array of Postgres features, and others were badly broken.
3.2.1 No Aggregates Within CASE (#20)
In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.4, aggregate expressions like COUNT(*) were not supported within CASE expressions.
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN COUNT(*) = 2
      THEN 'CASE_COUNT_STAR_OK'
      ELSE 'CASE_COUNT_STAR_BAD'
  END
FROM t;
This threw Error: cannot evaluate wildcard expression. ParticleDB gained support for this feature (#20) by version 1.1.18.6.
3.2.2 Unsupported Exponentiation (#28)
ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.8 did not support the Postgres exponentiation operator:
root=> SELECT 2 ^ 3;
ERROR:  unsupported binary operator: PGExp
Version 1.1.18.9 added support for the ^ operator (#28).
3.2.3 Malformed Responses for Prepared Statements (#2)
In ParticleDB 1.1.4 through 1.1.18.9, any attempt to execute a prepared statement using the Postgres JDBC driver caused an exception like Execution error (NoSuchElementEx

title: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts - Parameter
content:
Labs
Close
Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link.
Mukul Goyal
Oct 28, 2026
12 mins
October 26, 2026
Fixed
P1
Severity
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.
An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.
We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.
The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.
OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.
The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.
Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation
Victim opens the public share
HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page
JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session
Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:
read private chats and files, change the account
Technical walkthrough
It started with a graph and a Preview
The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?
ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.
At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.
The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.
Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.
That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.
MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.
The message that should not have worked
The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:
top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "update-setting",
  layouts: [{
    label: "Compatibility",
    layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }]
  }]
}, "*");

top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "show",
  animate: false
}, "*");
parameter
MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.
When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.
This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run.
The next step was an iframe using srcdoc, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:
<iframe srcdoc="..."></iframe>
parameter
MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.
Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP
ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.
YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:
https://www.youtube.com/oembed?callback=globalThis.__marker=31337;void
parameter
The response began like this:
// API callback
globalThis.__marker=31337;void({
  "error": {
    "code": 400,
    "message": "Invalid JSONP callback name: ..."
  }
});
parameter
Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.
We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.
Turning a lab bug into one public link
So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.
We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.
However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.
The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:
A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page.
A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.
The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.
We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.
The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.
The public share modified the real ChatGPT page
At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.
An alert was not enough
At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.
The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:
GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2
This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.
Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.
We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.
Controlled proof that private conversation data could leave the victim's session
The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.
Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.
What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed
The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.
Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:
MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity.
The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.
OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.
The defensive lessons are fairly simple:
A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission.
Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML.
Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame.
CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.
This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.
Timeline
Date Event
October 13, 2026 Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code.
October 14 Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript.
October 16 Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click.
October 17 Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh.
October 18 Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program.
October 19 Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof.
October 21 OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1.
October 22 OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated.
October 23 CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained.
October 26 OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.
Technical notes
The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.
The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:
window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.data?.type !== "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message") return;
  if (!validateOrigin(event.origin, this.originValidator)) return;
  this.handleMessage(event.data, event.source);
});

if (message.action === "update-setting" && message.layouts) {
  this.layouts = message.layouts;
}
parameter
Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:
keyboardContainer.innerHTML = MathfieldElement.createHTML(keyboardHTML);
parameter
createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

title: The Duty of a Scholar
content:
The Duty of a Scholar
On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.
There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.
This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.
Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.
In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.
Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done inefficiently. As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.
Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.
In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:
The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!
The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.
Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.
Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.
This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.
In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.
It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar.
