title: Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts - Parameter
content:
Labs
Close
Do the Math: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
By bypassing ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy, our research team was able to take over anyone's account simply by sending them a link.
Mukul Goyal
Oct 28, 2026
12 mins
October 26, 2026
Fixed
P1
Severity
In October 2026, we found a way to turn an ordinary public ChatGPT share into attacker-controlled JavaScript running inside the signed-in session of whoever opened it.
An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user. When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt.com with access to the victim's authenticated web session.
We confirmed that this code could enumerate the victim's conversation list, retrieve content from a private conversation that had never been shared with the attacker, and send data from that conversation to an external server. The payload was not limited to modifying the page or displaying an alert—it could directly call ChatGPT's authenticated APIs as the victim, essentially allowing us to take over the victim's ChatGPT account.
The victim did not need to install an App, join a Project, paste code, or open developer tools. Opening the shared link was the only required action.
OpenAI fixed the issue on October 26 and classified the report as P1.
The chain started with two features that looked harmless on their own: a graph and an HTML Preview.
Attacker publishes a ChatGPT conversation
Victim opens the public share
HTML Preview crosses into the main chatgpt.com page
JavaScript runs in the victim's signed-in session
Any action on chatgpt.com as the victim:
read private chats and files, change the account
Technical walkthrough
It started with a graph and a Preview
The question that started this research was simple: if Preview code was boxed into a different website, what could it still talk to?
ChatGPT can turn an HTML code block into a small working webpage using its Preview feature. Since that page may contain arbitrary code, ChatGPT sensibly runs it inside a restricted frame on a different web address. The Preview can run JavaScript, but the browser treats it as a different website, so it cannot directly inspect the signed-in ChatGPT page around it.
At first, this isolation appeared to work exactly as intended. Code inside the Preview could not read parent.document, which is the main ChatGPT page. That should have been the end of it.
The conversation also contained a normal interactive graph. Behind the scenes, the graph loaded a math library called MathLive. Loading it did more than draw the graph: it also installed a listener in the main ChatGPT page for messages related to MathLive's on-screen keyboard.
Browsers call the relevant API postMessage. It is a legitimate way for two frames to exchange information even when the browser prevents them from reading each other's pages. You can think of it as a mail slot: the restricted Preview cannot walk into the main page, but it can still drop a message through the slot.
That is safe only if the receiver checks who sent the message.
MathLive did not make that check for the setting we were interested in. Its listener accepted a message that changed the virtual keyboard layout, and that layout was allowed to contain HTML. The graph had installed the receiver; the Preview gave us an untrusted sender. Two unrelated features had accidentally created a path across the sandbox.
The message that should not have worked
The Preview sent two messages. The first replaced a virtual keyboard layout with our HTML. The second told MathLive to show the keyboard, causing it to render the new layout:
top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "update-setting",
  layouts: [{
    label: "Compatibility",
    layers: [{ id: "compatibility", markup }]
  }]
}, "*");

top.postMessage({
  type: "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message",
  action: "show",
  animate: false
}, "*");
parameter
MathLive recognized the public message type, but its top-level controller used an origin policy of none, which meant it accepted messages from any web address. It also did not require the update-setting message to come from a previously approved window. Anyone who could reach the listener and knew the message format could replace the layout.
When the keyboard opened, MathLive joined the supplied layout into an HTML string and assigned it to innerHTML in the real ChatGPT page. A helper named createHTML initially looked like it might sanitize the value. It did not; it marked the string as trusted and passed our HTML through unchanged.
This was exciting, but we still did not have JavaScript execution. Script tags inserted through innerHTML do not automatically run.
The next step was an iframe using srcdoc, a browser feature that lets an embedded frame carry its HTML directly in an attribute:
<iframe srcdoc="..."></iframe>
parameter
MathLive inserted this frame into the main ChatGPT document without a sandbox attribute. That gave us two useful properties. First, srcdoc created a fresh document where an external script could execute. Second, because the main ChatGPT page created the frame, the browser gave it the https://chatgpt.com web identity. Code inside the new frame could therefore access the parent page.
Bypassing CSP with YouTube JSONP
ChatGPT's Content Security Policy, or CSP, stopped us again. CSP controls which scripts a page may load, and the policy correctly blocked inline JavaScript. It did, however, allow scripts from YouTube.
YouTube's oEmbed endpoint supported a JSONP-style callback parameter. JSONP responses are JavaScript rather than ordinary JSON. The endpoint tried to reject an invalid callback, but it placed the callback into the response before returning its validation error:
https://www.youtube.com/oembed?callback=globalThis.__marker=31337;void
parameter
The response began like this:
// API callback
globalThis.__marker=31337;void({
  "error": {
    "code": 400,
    "message": "Invalid JSONP callback name: ..."
  }
});
parameter
Ending our callback with ;void made the object appended by YouTube harmless. Since YouTube was already allowed by ChatGPT's CSP, the browser loaded this response as a script and ran our callback inside the new frame.
We now had arbitrary JavaScript running as chatgpt.com. The original Preview was still isolated on its separate web address; we had crossed the boundary by convincing a trusted component in the main page to create a new, unsandboxed document for us.
Turning a lab bug into one public link
So far, this was a useful sandbox escape, but the first working version was not a convincing real-world attack. It used a researcher-controlled ChatGPT App as the sender. A victim would have needed to connect or invoke that App first.
We next tried delivering the payload through a native HTML attachment. ChatGPT opened the attachment inside the same sandboxed Preview, so it could send the malicious MathLive messages.
However, when we exported the conversation as a public share, the attachment remained but the earlier graph did not. The graph was essential because it loaded MathLive and installed the vulnerable message listener in the main page. Without it, the attachment could still send the messages, but nothing was listening to or processing them.
The breakthrough was putting both pieces directly into one ordinary public conversation:
A genuine graph initialized MathLive in the main page.
A later assistant-authored HTML Preview sent the two messages.
The resulting /share/<id> link preserved the complete chain for another user. The attacker could deliver it the same way they would send any shared ChatGPT conversation—through email, chat, a support ticket, or a social post. The victim did not need to install anything, join the attacker's workspace, or authenticate through an attacker-controlled flow. They just had to visit the attacker's shared ChatGPT URL.
We observed two versions of the interaction. In the most stable reproduction, the victim opened the share and clicked ChatGPT's normal Preview button once. We later marked the HTML block as previewable so that ChatGPT opened it automatically. In that version, opening the link was the victim's only click. We reproduced the automatic path three times in a separate account, including after a hard refresh, with the alert appearing after roughly 4.5 seconds.
The graph and Preview loaded independently, so the payload could occasionally send its message before MathLive was ready. The final carrier handled that race by retrying the same two messages for a limited period. A guard in the main page ensured that the private-conversation proof and outbound request ran only once.
The public share modified the real ChatGPT page
At this point, the public share could display an alert identified by the browser as coming from chatgpt.com and could add a banner to the main page. That proved where our code was running. It did not yet show why the bug mattered.
An alert was not enough
At this point, displaying an alert was the least interesting thing the exploit could do. The JavaScript was running as chatgpt.com, which meant it could interact with ChatGPT using the same authenticated context as the normal web application.
The payload read the session information already available to the page and used it to call ChatGPT's conversation APIs. First, it enumerated the victim's recent conversations. It could then request message data for a selected private conversation:
GET /backend-api/conversations?...&limit=20&order=updated&offset=0
GET /backend-api/conversations/<conversation-id>?num_turns=2
This was direct authenticated API access, not scraping text that happened to be visible on screen. The target conversation was unrelated to the malicious share and had never been shared with the attacker.
Once the response was available to the injected JavaScript, sending data off-site was straightforward. The payload created an ordinary image request to a server we controlled.
We deliberately sent only a small piece of the response off-site. The injected code had already received the authenticated conversation response and could read its contents, so the vulnerability was not limited to that value.
Controlled proof that private conversation data could leave the victim's session
The result was a practical cross-user data-theft primitive. A malicious public conversation could execute inside another user's signed-in ChatGPT session, enumerate private conversations, retrieve private message content, and send selected data to an attacker-controlled server.
Because the code ran with the web application's authenticated access, its reach was not inherently limited to the conversation endpoints used in our proof. Other data and actions exposed through ChatGPT's authenticated frontend APIs sat inside the same security boundary. Essentially, we could perform any action on behalf of the victim's ChatGPT account.
What went wrong and what OpenAI fixed
The Preview sandbox itself worked. Code inside Preview could not directly read the ChatGPT page. The problem was that another component in the main page was willing to accept its instructions.
Three design decisions turned that mistake into a full exploit:
MathLive accepted a state-changing message without proving which frame sent it.
The message format allowed raw HTML to be supplied as keyboard-layout data.
That HTML could create an unsandboxed document that inherited the chatgpt.com identity.
The YouTube response was the final workaround for CSP, not the root cause. Blocking only that endpoint would have removed one path to JavaScript while still leaving an untrusted Preview able to insert HTML into ChatGPT.
OpenAI reproduced both the JavaScript execution and the private-conversation proof. The fix was rolled out across two versions of ChatGPT's web frontend. During the rollout, CSP changes blocked part of the original chain while one version still needed an update. On October 26, OpenAI confirmed that both versions now rejected the cross-frame MathLive messages used by the report and marked the issue resolved.
The defensive lessons are fairly simple:
A message receiver should verify both the sender's web address and the exact window that was given permission.
Cross-window settings should not contain raw HTML.
Dynamically created documents should remain sandboxed when their content can be influenced by an untrusted frame.
CSP should be a backup control, not the only barrier after attacker-controlled HTML reaches the main site.
This bug was interesting because every individual feature looked reasonable. Preview was isolated. Graphs could load a math keyboard. Frames could exchange messages. CSP allowed a major media provider. Public conversations could be shared. The vulnerability appeared only when all of those features were combined in one page.
Timeline
Date Event
October 13, 2026 Confirmed the MathLive message-to-HTML path against ChatGPT's production code.
October 14 Reproduced the chain through the normal UI and upgraded the fixed alert to arbitrary JavaScript.
October 16 Confirmed public-share delivery between separate accounts and workspaces with one Preview click.
October 17 Confirmed automatic Preview from share navigation and reproduced it after a hard refresh.
October 18 Submitted the report to OpenAI's bug bounty program.
October 19 Added the controlled private-chat disclosure proof.
October 21 OpenAI reproduced the issue; severity was raised from the initial P2 triage to P1.
October 22 OpenAI reported one web frontend fixed while the second was still being updated.
October 23 CSP changes blocked part of the chain while one frontend update remained.
October 26 OpenAI confirmed both frontends rejected the reported messages, resolved the issue, and awarded a total bounty of $5,000.
Technical notes
The main story above contains the complete exploit chain. The details below are included for readers who want to follow the production code and payload transformations more closely.
The relevant deminified control flow was equivalent to:
window.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.data?.type !== "mathlive#virtual-keyboard-message") return;
  if (!validateOrigin(event.origin, this.originValidator)) return;
  this.handleMessage(event.data, event.source);
});

if (message.action === "update-setting" && message.layouts) {
  this.layouts = message.layouts;
}
parameter
Layout normalization preserved layouts[].layers[].markup. Showing the keyboard eventually performed the equivalent of:
keyboardContainer.innerHTML = MathfieldElement.createHTML(keyboardHTML);
parameter
createHTML acted as an identity or Trusted Types wrapper, not a sanitizer. Trusted Types can restrict who assigns to an HTML sink, but an identity policy does not make an attacker-controlled string safe.

title: Edgar Allan Poe is the most influential American writer. It’s time to admit it.
content:
BOOKS
Edgar Allan Poe, Quintessential American Writer
It’s time to acknowledge just how influential he was.
BY LAURA MILLER
FOLLOW LAURA MILLER
OCT 25, 20265:40 AM
Sepia Times/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
COMMENT
COPY LINK
GIFT STORY
Sign up for the Slatest to get the most insightful analysis, criticism, and advice out there, delivered to your inbox daily.
Who is the quintessential American writer? Whenever anyone starts kicking around that question, some predictable names turn up: Mark Twain, Herman Melville, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway, Toni Morrison. Rarely, though, does anyone mention Edgar Allan Poe, even though Poe is arguably the most influential American writer of all. In fact, after poking around online, I found just one site that listed Poe as No. 1 in the “Top 10 American Writers,” an MIT-affiliated outfit called Pantheon.world that claims to use “biographical data to expose patterns of human collective memory” via a “slow and painful process.” Whatever that means, Pantheon draws from international sources, and without a doubt, Poe is more highly revered abroad than in his own homeland.
Emily Ogden’s Darkness Becomes Bright: On the Brief Life and Immortal Art of Edgar Allan Poe is a step toward correcting that. This slim, sinuous collection of essays on Poe’s influence, published earlier this fall, braids together strands of memoir, biography, and literary criticism to make a case for Poe as a writer whose “fundamental theme is the human cry issuing from desperate extremity,” and whose global impact has been formidable. A professor of English at the University of Virginia (a school Poe himself attended for one term back in 1826), Ogden writes that, “in the space of Poe’s works, some of us have been able to tolerate ourselves as we actually are: limited, cruel, perverse, and mortal, but, for all that, still glittering with a heavenly light.” To illustrate this, she explores what three non-American writers—the Argentinian novelist Julio Cortázar, the psychoanalyst Marie Bonaparte, and the French poet Charles Baudelaire—found revelatory and essential in Poe’s writing.
It’s easy to see, though, why Poe doesn’t fit within many Americans’ notion of our literature. With the exception of a short, early, and minor work, The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, he wrote no novels, the most exalted literary form during the 20th century, when the nation’s literary culture reached its maturity. Poe’s most famous tales and poetry make no effort to depict American life or social issues, and tend to take place in fantastical and vaguely European settings: moldering manor houses or the dungeons of the Spanish Inquisition. In fact, the settings of most of Poe’s stories feel detached from any real-world locations. They are the stuff of dreams, or rather, nightmares.
Join Slate Plus to keep reading: “One Literary Giant Is Rarely Associated With His Homeland. Make No Mistake: He’s the Most Influential American Writer of All.”
Unlock unlimited reading, bonus podcast episodes, ad-free listening, every Slate Game, and more. Try 3 months for just $5 per month.
Join Slate Plus
Already a member?
Sign in here.
Poe’s work, furthermore, seems in deliberate, even flagrant, contrast with what were once regarded as the great themes of American literature: the freedom of self-reinvention promised by a new society and its frontier, exploration, rugged individualism, and the struggle to conquer nature. Where other writers saw the American landscape as offering room to prove oneself and forge a destiny unfettered by the past, Poe’s tales and poems are claustrophobic and fatalistic. Tombs, prisons, catacombs, and walled-up alcoves abound in his fiction. Even when his characters aren’t physically confined, they are trapped by some inescapable doom: madness, guilt, grief, or the plague that stalks the aristocratic revelers in “The Masque of the Red Death.” Instead of optimistic and outgoing—the European stereotype of Americans—they are morbid and withdrawn. Instead of persevering against all odds, they despair.
Darkness Becomes Bright: On the Brief Life and Immortal Art of Edgar Allan Poe

title: The Duty of a Scholar
content:
The Duty of a Scholar
On November 16th, 2004 — π years after arriving in Oxford — I submitted my doctoral thesis. My mind wasn't really on my thesis though; I was thinking about an issue I had noticed in recent Intel CPUs: The "Hyper-Threading" (simultaneous multithreading) feature they introduced in 2002 could leak information between execution threads via the cache state.
There was a joke at the time that although the National Security Agency had opened up in recent years and started taking their defensive role more seriously, the one aspect of cryptography which they would never discuss publicly was side channel attacks — and this itself constituted a side channel, revealing the importance they attributed to the field. Being active in computer security, and recognizing that the NSA knew a few things about the topic, my immediate priority was to determine whether the information leakage I had identified was sufficient to construct a practical cryptographic side channel. By mid-December I had a proof-of-concept exploit which stole enough bits of an RSA private key for the entire key to be reconstructed, and I turned my attention to the hard part of the problem: Quietly notifying security teams and working together to get the issue fixed before disclosing it publicly.
This became my occupation for the next six months. While my Oxonian contemporaries were making corrections to their theses and applying for jobs, I set those aside (much to the irritation of my supervisors): I had a responsibility, and it took priority over mere career considerations. As it turned out, being unemployed proved useful in early May, when Intel — rather irked by my impending publication — asked Yahoo to order me to withdraw the paper; Yahoo was very happy to reply that, unlike many FreeBSD developers, I was not in fact employed by them and they were not in a position to threaten to fire me. On May 13th, 2005, I presented my paper at BSDCan and published an advisory on the topic; advisories were published at the same time or soon thereafter by FreeBSD, NetBSD, Red Hat, SCO, and Ubuntu.
Anyone involved with open source software security will recognize the process of responsible disclosure (now widely called "coordinated disclosure", after some people in the industry struggled with the concept of responsibility), although the length of this particular process was unusual. If you find a security vulnerability, you shouldn't ignore it (or worse, sell it to bad actors); conversely, it's irresponsible to simply publish the vulnerability and hope that the good guys can fix it before the bad guys exploit it. Instead, you have a responsibility to identify who needs to know about the issue and to contact them — quietly — so they can get patches ready to distribute to their users the moment the issue becomes publicly known.
In this particular case, I was unusually able to put my life on hold: I was single, child-free, and, after defending my thesis and returning home to Canada, living rent-free in my (very tolerant) parents' basement. While I had some bills to cover — being a type 1 diabetic, I had to purchase insulin — living in Canada meant that I didn't need to worry about the risk of extraordinary costs from a hospital stay. Had I been living in the USA, I would have needed to prioritize seeking employment and medical insurance and likely would not have been able to discharge the duty which fate had thrust upon me.
Engineers, of course, are familiar with such duties: While the precise language varies from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, nearly all professional ethical codes include a requirement to act upon safety hazards regardless of whether any personal connection exists. Members of the IEEE commit, for example, "to hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public..." without that duty being limited to hazards arising from projects employing the Engineer in question: The duty "to disclose promptly" vests in any Engineer who recognizes that the hazard exists. As with responsible disclosure of software security vulnerabilities, however, the subject matter of this duty is limited in scope: There is no duty to report if work is being done inefficiently. As a legal duty this would be reasonable; but as a moral duty, I feel it sets the bar too low.
Engineering codes also often set out a process of escalation: In the common case of a licensed Engineer becoming aware of a hazard in a project they are working on, in the first instance they should report their concerns to their employer; only if that fails to yield results should they take more direct steps. This is both efficient and practical: Reporting an issue to someone who fails to act upon it isn't necessarily sufficient to discharge a duty, but conversely reporting everything broadly risks drowning out the few items which truly need broad attention. I routinely apply this same principle; for example, in 2009 I discovered that the Amazon EC2 firewall broke Path MTU Discovery by default and reported it to Amazon; but by November 2012 I concluded that Amazon was not going to address the problem, so I took to my blog to advise Amazon customers on how to fix Path MTU Discovery for themselves. (As it happened, Amazon fixed the bug a short time later.) While this was in no way a safety or computer security concern, I felt that, knowing what I did, I had an ethical duty to share that knowledge to help people who were affected by the issue.
In the Star Trek: The Next Generation episode "The First Duty", the late Patrick Stewart, speaking as Jean-Luc Picard, delivers a memorable speech about truth:
The first duty of every Starfleet officer is to the truth, whether it's scientific truth or historical truth or personal truth! It is the guiding principle on which Starfleet is based! If you can't find it within yourself to stand up and tell the truth about what happened, you don't deserve to wear that uniform!
The duty described here is a duty to uncover and not conceal the truth; while I agree with this duty, I don't think it goes far enough. To me, the duty includes actively seeking out people to whom the truth should be told. To hide behind "nobody asked" is to fail to fulfill the duty.
Much ink has been spilled by philosophers about duty and ethics, and the German Enlightenment philosopher Fichte in particular had some interesting comments to make in the fourth of his 1794 lectures, Über die Bestimmung des Gelehrten — often translated as The Vocation of the Scholar, which inspired the title of this essay. Fichte argues that Scholars have a particular relationship to knowledge: A Scholar "possesses his Knowledge not for himself, but for society". It is not proper for a Scholar to hoard knowledge; rather, Scholars have a duty to impart their knowledge to others — in Fichte's somewhat exaggerated view, to act as "the Teacher of the human race". On the other hand, it is unnecessary and inappropriate to enter with everyone into the "deep inquiries which he himself has been obliged to undertake"; rather, a Scholar relies upon others' trust in the Scholar's honesty when conveying the particular knowledge which is needed. Fichte notes that "[t]he Scholar will never be tempted to bring men to the adoption of his convictions by coercion or the use of physical force [...] neither will he deceive them". Scholars are not Plato's philosopher-kings; their duty is to provide the requisite knowledge, not to enforce what is done with that knowledge.
Now, I don't agree with Fichte on every point. Fichte considers Scholars to be the loftiest of all classes, and even invites each Scholar to consider themselves a "Priest of Truth"; living in rather more egalitarian times, I absolutely reject this framing. Nor do I accept Fichte's framing (in his preceding lecture, On the Distinction of Classes in Society) that the duty of Scholars to share knowledge arises from an obligation to render back to society what it has done for us; to me, the duty arises not from a debt to society, but rather attaches to knowledge itself, no matter who holds it.
This duty, naturally, is not unlimited. As Fichte notes, there is no duty to force people to act upon shared knowledge — indeed there is a moral obligation to accept everyone's freedom to choose how they act. Similarly, there is no duty to become a Cassandra: As with any gift, people are free to refuse the gift of knowledge, however unwise that might be; ultimately, if everyone who is able to act upon some knowledge has been made aware of it, the duty has been exhausted.
In modern vernacular, the terms "Scholar" and "Researcher" often overlap, but to me there is a very precise distinction: Researchers create new knowledge, while Scholars carry that knowledge to the people who need it — a narrower definition than that of Fichte, whose Scholars also carry a duty to strive to extend knowledge. Many people, of course, are both Researchers and Scholars; but there are plenty of people who perform research and publish papers without truly communicating their discoveries. The research paper which is published in a journal but never read is almost a cliché; but even papers which are read do not necessarily have the impact they deserve if they are read only by academics and not by anyone in a position to act upon the findings published. My undergraduate alma mater, Simon Fraser University — of which I have been a sitting Senator for over two decades — describes itself as "Canada's engaged university" and makes a point of valuing not just academic output but the work of connecting academic learning with the real world. A true Scholar, in my mind, is someone who feels bound by the duty of knowledge: To find the people with whom it should be shared.
It is for everyone to choose their own role in society, and not everyone feels every duty the same way; for that matter, just as my experience in 2005 would have been different had I needed to obtain medical insurance, not everyone is able to act upon a duty, no matter how much they feel it. But for myself, I choose the life and duty of a Scholar.

title: Let’s Build a Brain
content:
MYRIAD
Let’s Build a Brain
By Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee
The world is full of surprising behavior: Beavers building dams, songbirds singing, spiders building webs, and you reading this article.
All of these behaviors are orchestrated by neurons firing in the brain. But how exactly do collections of neurons create these complex behaviors?
This is a huge question that researchers are still working on. But over the last half century, neuroscientists have solved some pieces of this puzzle.
In this article, we’ll build a tiny creature called a spark, and we’ll give it a very simple brain. As you’ll see, even this tiny brain can create rich and unexpected behaviors.
Light eaters
Suppose this spark feeds on light. Its goal in life is to reach the light.
The light-hungry spark needs a way to sense the world. So we’ll give it a rudimentary eye — a single neuron that detects brightness and converts it into electrical pulses.
It also needs a way to move. So we’ll give it another neuron that can wiggle a flipper.
By wiring the first sensory neuron to the second motor neuron, we’ve just assembled our first neural circuit:
The anatomy of a spark
With this simple circuit, the spark wiggles its flipper in proportion to the amount of light.
Can it find the light?
If the sparks happen to face the light, they’re drawn towards it. But most of the time, they miss.
Over time, their paths look like this:
Only a few paths cross the light. Clearly, we can do a lot better…
Adding an eye
Here’s the problem: While the spark can speed up, it can’t steer. With one eye and one flipper, it only moves in one direction. But we need it to turn.
What if we give it another eye and flipper?
With two eyes, the spark can now sense whether the light is to its left or right. Now, it moves like this:
Hmm… that didn’t work. Instead of steering towards the light, it steered away from it!
If you didn’t know how their brains work, you might think that they fear light.
Why do they avoid the light? Well, if the light were to the spark’s left, then its left eye would sense more brightness, which means that its left flipper would wiggle faster, and this would cause it to turn right, away from the light. Conversely, if the light were to its right, then it would veer left.
A crossed connection
But there’s a clever way to make this spark steer towards the light instead.
All we have to do is cross its connections. That is, we wire its left eye to its right flipper, and its right eye to its left flipper.
Now, it moves like this:
With this simple wiring change, it can finally steer towards the light.
But if you watch these sparks for a while, you’ll notice that there’s a problem.
While they can reach the light, they don’t slow down near it. Instead, they charge towards it like comets plunging towards the sun.
If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they’re attacking the light.
Becoming inhibited
Why do they attack the light? The problem lies in the type of connection that we used.
To see why, we need to go back to our original spark. Remember how its flipper moved faster when the light got brighter? That’s because its eye and flipper were connected with an excitatory connection — where more input leads to more output.
If the light were a food source, then this spark would accelerate towards it, but it wouldn’t stop to enjoy its lunch.
Instead, we want the spark to slow down as it approaches the light. That is, we want its motion to be inhibited by light.
We can solve this by swapping out the excitatory connection for an inhibitory connection — one where more input leads to less output.
With the original excitatory connection, the spark overshoots the light. With the inhibitory one, it slows down and gently comes to a stop.
Finding the light
Now let’s bring back the original two-eyed spark, but this time with inhibitory connections between its eyes and flippers.
Now, the flipper closer to the light moves slower, while the flipper on the opposite side moves faster, and this makes the spark turn towards the light.
Drag the light to move it around.
Hooray! It can finally steer to the light and come to a stop. You can move the light in the graphic above (or the one below) to watch the sparks react.
Drag the light to move it around.
They move as if they’re magnetically attracted to the light. If you didn’t know how their brains work, now you might think that they love light.
We’ve now seen four very different behaviors, each achieved by making small changes to the neural circuitry of our virtual creatures.
Attraction
Fear
Aggression
Love
Note: We’ve added a small amount of noise to the simulation to make the paths look more organic.
If you saw creatures behaving like this in the wild, you might attribute some rudimentary intelligence to them.
But we’ve just shown you how this apparent intelligence arises from the bottom up, with just four neurons and two connections. There’s no magic here. In this view, behavior emerges from neural circuits.
And if a brain with just four neurons can do all this, imagine what your brain can achieve with nearly 100 billion neurons.
Adding variation
We can take this one step further.
In each of the simulations so far, the sparks all had identical brains. But biology is full of variation: No two brains are the same.
If we allow the connections between neurons to vary in strength, then each spark can react differently to the light.
They now have different preferences: The yellower sparks seem to love light more, while the redder sparks keep a cautious distance.
Drag the light to move it around.
Just as a thermostat sets a preferred temperature, their brain wiring now determines their preference for light.
If you squint very hard at this, you might be able to see the rudiments of how our brains encode preferences, such as a love for spicy food or an aversion to smelly cheese.
Of course, biology is far more complex than these simplified sparks. We intentionally gave them very simple brains, so that we can understand how every part works.
Their brains are also frozen in time. In reality, brains can learn: They alter their wiring to gain new skills such as learning to walk, ride a bicycle, or play a piano.
In the next article, we’ll watch this learning process in action, and see how these sparks rewire their brains to find the light.
Share this article
Learn more
Thanks for reading Myriad, a blog by Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee exploring how minds emerge from matter.
Arka is an associate professor of neuroscience at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory in New York. Check out his lab’s research on how a singing mouse in the cloud forests of Costa Rica got its song.
Aatish is a science journalist with a Ph.D. in physics. Previously, he was a graphics editor at The New York Times. Follow Aatish’s work for more visually-immersive interactive explanations about science.
The sparks that we assembled in this article are based on a series of thought experiments by the neuroscientist Valentino Braitenberg described in his delightfully quirky 1984 book Vehicles: Experiments in Synthetic Psychology.
While the one-eyed sparks may look peculiar, it’s possible that you and I descended from a one-eyed cyclops-like creature that lived 560 million years ago.

Introduction
It is a well-known fact that the existence of Quines are a consequence of Kleene’s 2nd recursion theorem. I was curious about how easy or difficult it was to use this construction in practice, so I decided to try to formalize it.
One of the virtues of formalization is that it naturally motivates the mathematician to structure their definitions and proofs in a clearer and more concise fashion. The pain of a clunky definition or ill-structured argument is actually felt, and so the goals of expedient proofs and well-structured proofs often align. Far from being a mechanical chore, the act of formalization can actually be a source of insight and creativity (incidentally, this is why I think the popular view of formal verification as a mere exercise in transcription misses the mark).
With this in mind, I hoped that I could find or develop a clean formalization that could shed some light on a theorem that I was only familiar with on rather hand-wavy terms. During my search, I was fortunate enough to uncover this excellent preprint that laid out how to perform this construction in the untyped lambda calculus. For the remainder of this post I will sketch out the proof from this preprint and offer some motivation for why we might chose to present the theorem this way.

Models of Computation
Traditional presentations of computability theory tend to adopt a reductionist attitude where all discrete structures (pairs, lists, syntactic objects, etc.) are just natural numbers. This necessitates many tedious encodings whose details the presenter would prefer to not mention, and thus we get a lot of hand-waving.
This sort of presentation is understandable to an extent. If you are only interested in arriving at deep/advanced results, it makes sense that you would not want to waste too much time with the low-level details when, after all, “all these models of computation are equivalent” anyway. However, this sort of approach runs the risk of engendering a sort of nihilism with respect to formal systems. All systems are equally arbitrary, ugly, etc. so why bother even studying them in detail?
There is a subfield that takes matters of structure in formal systems more seriously: Proof theory. One of the big takeaways I received from proof theory is that there can be significant content found in the way we structure our formal systems. So, returning to computability theory, it is appropriate that our search for a model that takes structure seriously, we arrive at the most proof-theoretic model of computation, the lambda calculus.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Scan a Linux panic QR code with ZXingReader and decompress its crash log.
  ./decode-kernel-panic.py screenshot.png -o panic.log
"""
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
from urllib.parse import parse_qs, urlsplit
import zlib
def decode_panic_url(url):
    """Decode the kernel's z parameter: 17 decimal digits per 7 little-endian bytes.
    Format reference: https://github.com/kdj0c/panic_report
    """
    parts = urlsplit(url)
    parameters = parse_qs(parts.query, keep_blank_values=True)
    if "z" not in parameters:
        parameters = parse_qs(parts.fragment.lstrip("?"), keep_blank_values=True)
    if "z" not in parameters:
        raise ValueError("QR code URL has no compressed panic data (z parameter)")
    if len(parameters["z"]) != 1:
        raise ValueError("QR code URL has multiple z parameters")
    digits = parameters["z"][0]
    if not digits or not digits.isascii() or not digits.isdecimal():
        raise ValueError("panic data must contain only decimal digits")
    # A final, partial group uses fewer digits and bytes.
    byte_counts = {3: 1, 5: 2, 8: 3, 10: 4, 13: 5, 15: 6, 17: 7}
    compressed = bytearray()
    for offset in range(0, len(digits), 17):
        chunk = digits[offset:offset + 17]
        if len(chunk) not in byte_counts:
            raise ValueError("invalid length of encoded panic data")
        try:
            compressed.extend(int(chunk).to_bytes(byte_counts[len(chunk)], "little"))
        except OverflowError as exc:
            raise ValueError("encoded panic data contains an out-of-range chunk") from exc
    return zlib.decompress(compressed)
def scan_image(image):
    if not image.is_file():
        raise ValueError(f"image does not exist or is not a file: {image}")
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["ZXingReader", "-formats", "QRCode", "-json", str(image.resolve())],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
        )
    except FileNotFoundError as exc:
        raise ValueError("ZXingReader is required; install it and put it on PATH") from exc
    if result.returncode != 0:
        detail = result.stderr.strip() or "no readable QR code found"
        raise ValueError(f"ZXingReader failed: {detail}")
    if not result.stdout.strip():
        raise ValueError("no readable QR code found")
    try:
        qr = json.loads(result.stdout)
    except json.JSONDecodeError as exc:
        raise ValueError("expected one QR code in ZXingReader's JSON output") from exc
    if not isinstance(qr, dict) or not isinstance(qr.get("Text"), str):
        raise ValueError("ZXingReader returned no QR code text")
    return qr["Text"]
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="Scan a Linux panic screenshot with ZXingReader and decompress its log.",
        epilog="Requires Python 3 and ZXingReader. Decoding runs locally without network access.",
    )
    parser.add_argument("image", type=Path, help="screenshot or photo containing the panic QR code")
    parser.add_argument("-o", "--output", type=Path, help="write the log to a file instead of stdout")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        if args.output and args.output.resolve() == args.image.resolve():
            raise ValueError("output must differ from the input image")
        log = decode_panic_url(scan_image(args.image))
        if args.output:
            args.output.write_bytes(log)
        else:
            sys.stdout.buffer.write(log)
    except BrokenPipeError:
        # Allow commands such as `decode-kernel-panic screenshot.png | head`.
        import os
        os.dup2(os.open(os.devnull, os.O_WRONLY), sys.stdout.fileno())
        return 0
    except (OSError, ValueError, zlib.error) as exc:
        print(f"{parser.prog}: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1
    return 0
if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

title: AI text watermarking and quality loss - Keyvan's blog
content:
AI text watermarking and quality loss
AUG 24, 2026
5
1
1
Share
After the EU AI Act’s transparency guidelines went into effect, and following the announcement that most major AI labs will soon be watermarking their text output to comply, there has been some debate about how much of an impact this is going to have, if any, on the quality of the text produced by AI models.
Since the focus of AI labs shifted to code production, I think the written output of the models has gotten much worse.1 But it’s still interesting to try to understand if watermarking could make it even worse.
I found the discussion around technology writer John Gruber’s recent post, Anthropic’s ‘Watermark’ Text Adulteration in Claude Is a Perversion of Writing, very interesting.
On watermarking, Gruber wrote:
It’s unacceptable for a tool to sacrifice an iota of clarity, coherence, meaning, quality, etc. for the purpose of embedding hidden clues within the text to suggest its provenance.
He got a lot of pushback, with many debating how you would even measure quality, or define it.
But some argued that watermarking does not affect quality at all: it’s essentially just using different random numbers to generate the text. Daniel Jalkut, whom Gruber linked to in his follow-up, published a piece titled AI Can’t Adulterate its Own Writing, in which he wrote:
…there are also ways of tweaking the algorithm that would not diminish its randomness. For example if a random number generator routinely reversed the order of the digits in a generated number, the randomness would remain the same.
Similarly, in another discussion, someone described it as essentially swapping two faces of a die.
In a follow-up piece, Gruber wrote:
I hope that’s true. I believe it’s possible that it is true. I think it’s highly unlikely that it is true.
I think Gruber is right.
Quality loss across responses
Anthropic make a bold claim: “Watermarking does not impact the quality of Claude’s output.” The paper they link to and based their design on (Google’s SynthID-Text, published in Nature in 2024) assures everyone that the method “preserves response quality”.
So it’s easy to assume there’s been a lot of fuss over nothing, that they really are just swapping some random numbers around.
But their no-quality-impact claim, which they tested with humans, is based on single responses. Not the way millions of people actually use these systems: as back-and-forth conversations, over time, over multiple prompts and responses.
The 56-page supplementary PDF they link to at the bottom provides some more info on the method used, and it suggests the no-quality-impact claim isn’t telling the full story. Notably, it says that there is a “diversity/detectability trade-off”:
While single-sequence non-distortion guarantees the quality of each individual response, it does not necessarily preserve diversity across multiple responses
Okay, so what does that mean? They go on to explain:
when sampling several responses to the same prompt, the similarity between the responses is greater for the watermarked responses than the unwatermarked responses.
Now, if they had truly only swapped one set of random numbers for another, we would not be seeing any such difference compared to the unwatermarked responses.
They go on to write:
This could be problematic in scenarios where inter-response diversity is important, or could lower the overall quality of a system which generates many responses then selects the best one
Okay, so in their own words, it can “lower overall quality” after all. But nothing to worry about, because this would only concern you if you cared about “inter-response diversity”, for which they only provide one example: a system which generates and selects responses.
But “inter-response diversity” affects how most people use these systems too. Especially for writing tasks where you want creativity.
In response to Gruber’s point about sacrificed quality, some argued that the model has no notion of the best next word to use for what each individual is trying to convey in their specific work, and so we shouldn’t get too hung up on the next word choice. But then surely they’d agree that you, the individual, would know if it’s suitable or not once you see it.
Let’s say you prompt: “I don’t like the ending to this sentence. Please suggest a new one: [sentence].” The model suggests an alternative, but you don’t like it. No problem, hit the retry button. Well, now you’re affected by watermarking, because you have hit the “inter-response diversity” problem: like throwing a loaded die, you’ll see similar responses more than you would with an unwatermarked model.
Natzir Turrado, a technical consultant, actually tested this (article in Spanish) by reproducing SynthID-Text on an open model with the paper's settings and a watermark key. He asked the watermarked model five times to describe a memorable trip to a coastal town. Four of the five answers he got back opened in a near-identical way: “My heart still sings/dances when I think back to my trip to the quaint coastal town of…”. For the unwatermarked model, three opened in different ways.2
And though they don’t appear to have tested for it, the same thing that makes answers to the same prompt look similar could happen across different prompts too. The watermark only looks at a small sliding context window when choosing the next token, so any time two pieces of writing pass through the same short token sequence, they could be recreating the same context window, leading to a more predictable and less diverse output. And writing is full of identical short phrases that could trigger this behaviour.
Here’s another example of what this affects: one way people try to determine the confidence level of a response, to lower the chances of hallucinations, is to repeat the same prompt a number of times, to explore the different pathways the model takes. They then look at the results to see where the consensus lies. Well, this is also affected. With watermarking, you’re less able to trust the consensus you see forming, because the answers are now less independent: they’re steered by the watermark key.
What’s interesting is that while the SynthID paper points to the loss of quality across responses, I couldn’t find anywhere in the paper where they tested this particular aspect of the watermarking method with humans. If they didn’t, the wonderful human test results they point to did not involve testing the most affected part of the watermarking method.3
So it seems to me that they are sacrificing quality, by limiting the creative range of their models through watermarking, and they don’t think you’ll notice or care much.4
1
A pattern Jasmine Sun found looking at why AI models don't write well. Here’s what Katy Gero, a poet and computer scientist, had to say:
The same whimsicality that made GPT-2’s voice fresh also made it prone to other unpredictable behavior. “If you’re a big corporation like Google or OpenAI, you want a chatbot that’s going to make money. The chatbot that’s not going to make you money is the one that’s a weirdo,” Gero said.
2
Natzir Turrado pointed me to a reply he received on X from one of the SynthID paper’s authors, Sumanth Dathathri:
There's a lot of easy fixes to the diversity issue. I think if you tried the same prompt with Gemini/Claude many times, you'd get very diverse responses :)
It’s a bit ambiguous, but I wonder if his “easy fix” is shifting the problem to the user. It reads to me like he’s acknowledging that they’ve replaced the previous die with a loaded one, but the solution is just to roll it “many times” (my emphasis), and it’ll eventually land on each of its faces. If that is what he’s saying, why not admit that such a change does make the system worse than it was before for the user?
Turrado responded: “Curious: which easy fixes don’t trade off detection strength?”
No reply from Dathathri so far.
3
A recent paper recognised that this is an “understudied fundamental trade-off in LLM watermarks: quality-diversity-power, i.e., the trade-off between the quality of the watermarked text, the output diversity under the watermarking scheme, and the overall watermarking signal strength.”
4
There are ways to mitigate some of the effects to make them less noticeable to an individual using a chat app, e.g. by rotating watermark keys between each of their requests. But these are not fixes. They only dilute the effect, and have their own costs, e.g. making watermarking less effective on shorter texts, and more costly to detect. As another study pointed out: “achieving a perfect distortion-free watermark is impossible”.

title: Sculpture re-creates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup - Ars Technica
content:
THEIR CUP RUNNETH OVER
Sculpture re-creates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup
University of Sheffield researchers figured out how to re-create the 1,600-year-old glass recipe.
JENNIFER OUELLETTE – OCT 27, 2026 1:32 PM | 61
Credit: Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films

Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect.
The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007, when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point.
As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It’s also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals.
ARS VIDEO
How The Callisto Protocol's Team Designed Its Terrifying, Immersive Audio
When viewed in reflected light, the cup’s dichroic glass is green in color. British Museum
When viewed in transmitted light (backlit), the glass appears red. Chappsnet/CC BY 4.0
There is a key difference, however: The nanoparticles are embedded into the glass of the cup, whereas with a daguerreotype, they are sitting on top of a substrate, adding some reflection that does not occur with an artifact like the Lycurgus Cup. So the scattering of the particles has a strong dependence on the substrate. Also, if one coats the surface of a daguerreotype with a layer of gold, the colors shift more to the red side of the spectrum. That’s in keeping with a 19th-century trick called “gilding,” in which the photographer would apply a solution of gold salt to the image to achieve warmer tones and sharper contrast.
An elusive recipe
In 2020, Dutch researchers reproduced the green/red dichroic effect of the Lycurgus Cup in a 3D-printable nanocomposite material by embedding small amounts of silver and gold nanoparticles of the proper size and shapes. But nobody had yet devised a consistent, replicable recipe. University of Sheffield scientists Lisa Hollands and Caroline Jackson—the latter an expert on Roman glass—worked together to come up with one, experimenting with different furnace types, materials, oxygen levels, and at one point including sugar in the mix.
“I knew that making a glass of this type was likely to be a complex task, as it is not just a case of adding nanoparticles to glass,” said Hollands. “I’ve studied and worked with glass for over 25 years, so I used the knowledge and experience I’ve gained, coupled with a modern scientific understanding of what I was trying to achieve—although if the Romans could have seen me experimenting, they’d probably laugh and ask: ‘Why does she not know how to make this?’”
A contemporary glass sculpture paying homage to its intricate ancient twin using glass made in the Sheffield melting shop Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films
UK glass artist Elliot Walker created the new piece using the Sheffield recipe Ed Cartledge, Sort of Films
The experimentation paid off when Hollands found a mix that produced glass with the desired optical effects, appearing green in reflected light, red when backlit. Her initial glass piece was exhibited at LightFest, which is part of Molecular Photonic Breadboards, a UK project geared toward designing new materials that harness the power of light for sustainable technologies. Project leaders next decided to commission UK glass artist Elliott Walker—the S2 winner of Netflix’s Blown Away competition—to create a contemporary sculpture to pay homage to the original Lycurgus Cup.
“It is a very rare thing to have the opportunity to work with glass developed from ancient mixtures and recipes, and it is always a very exciting one,” said Walker. “You can really get an idea of how the glass makers of the past would have adapted to this sort of glass; it’s like shaking their hands. I wanted to keep the sculpture quite classical in form and to carry through the original story of Lycurgus shown on the cup, but we needed a blown element within this to really show the dichroic glass. The piece is a blend of the Lycurgus story and the Farnese Atlas sculpture, with the globe replaced by a cup.”
The public will get its chance to see Walker’s sculpture in person when it is unveiled at the Millennium Gallery next month during the University of Sheffield’s Festival of the Mind. After that, it will have a permanent home on display at the university’s Turner Museum of Glass.
JENNIFER OUELLETTE SENIOR WRITER
Jennifer is a senior writer at Ars Technica with a particular focus on where science meets culture, covering everything from physics and related interdisciplinary topics to her favorite films and TV series. Jennifer lives in Baltimore with her spouse, physicist Sean M. Carroll, and their two cats, Ariel and Caliban.

title: GitHub - kerlenton/bootgpt: A language model that lives in a boot sector · GitHub
content:
bootgpt
A neural network that boots your PC.
The MBR is 512 bytes of hand written asm. It loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from the next 23 sectors and runs it in 16-bit real mode on a 386. No OS, no C runtime, nothing. The machine wakes up and dreams a Linux boot log: timestamps, PCI bars, ACPI events for hardware that never existed.
Build thread: https://x.com/krlntn/status/2116514628457185757
With 8 chars of context and one hidden layer this is roughly the quality you get:
[  2.283888] pci 0000:01:01.4: [1b36:0a35] ryndrde c4128 6422 Vveine
[  1.953886] pci 0000:01:1f.2: reg 0x10: [mem 0x7e4515e5-0x2d766c27] usbbore: reg
[  0.206596] Command line: BOOT_IMAGE=/vmlinu -5.5.2-1-generic gcc version 13.3.0, GNU ld ...
[  1.815765] ACPI: PCI Interrupt Link [LNKA: v/s.xos212
[  1.883084] NET: Registered protocol family 16
Run it
brew install nasm qemu
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install numpy
./build.sh
./run.sh
disk.img is a normal boot image. dd it to a USB stick and boot any BIOS box if you have one. It only reads its own sectors.
Pieces
corpus_gen.py makes 3 MB of fake dmesg. One kernel version and one disk per boot session, because real boot logs repeat themselves and that repetition is what makes a tiny model look sane.
train.py trains the model (char embeddings, one hidden layer, softmax) and quantizes everything to int8 with power-of-two scales, so the boot sector can do the whole forward pass with imul and a single idiv. The script also simulates the exact integer math the asm will run, LCG sampler included, so the Python output and the boot sector output can be diffed. They match char for char.
boot.asm is the entire runtime: int 13h to load weights, int 10h to print, a softclip activation done with cdq/idiv, argmax sampling with timer seeded noise. Any keypress reboots the machine.
record.py records the demo gif from headless QEMU through the monitor socket. No window involved.
The boot sector is code only. Strings, weights and the vocab table all live in the data sectors, it was the only way to fit inference plus BIOS plumbing into 510 bytes.
Prior art
The boot sector genre is old and glorious. Oscar Toledo put chess, a whole OS and even a BASIC interpreter in there, other people did a C compiler, all inside 512 bytes. His book on boot sector games is a good read.
The closest neighbor is sectorllm, which boots a real llama2 transformer (5 layers, attention, the works) from about 1.2 KB of real mode asm, running Karpathy's stories260K model. sectorlisp-nn runs a TensorFlow-trained network during boot on a Lisp interpreter, and there are UEFI apps that boot straight into llama-class models on modern hardware.
bootgpt takes the other extreme: the whole engine fits in the 510-byte MBR itself, weights and strings live in the following sectors, and the model is not a general story teller but a tiny char-level net trained for exactly one thing, hallucinating the boot log of the machine it wakes up on.

title: HackerTube – karpathy
content:
HackerTube
31 Oct, 2026
It was Friday night at 11pm, I was tired, I went to YouTube to watch something and realized that I was looking at an enshittified wall of slop. Insanely exaggerated thumbnails, dumb recommendations of the same tired topics, truly terrible idiocracy-grade content. I'm sure this algorithm works well for the median person on the internet, but it definitely does not work for me. So this morning (Saturday) I took a hold of my Opus 5.5 and gave it the task: Let's write our own YouTube clone based on whatever videos have been recommended on Hacker News. And Opus came back with: hackertube.org!
Opus downloaded all comments of HackerNews, filtered them, ran Sonnet over them in a Workflow (Claude Code feature), got rid of spam, and narrowed everything down to 40K comments recommending a YouTube video. In total, we get 6,454 YouTube videos that have been recommended by a few people on HN from 2007-2026 across 150 topics. Then we wrap it up in a YouTube UI, get a domain, push to a VPS, secure, harden, optimize and voila!
HackerTube:
Contains quality content
Uses the 50% thumbnail instead of the uploaded thumbnail
Custom and good ForYou recommendations without any user accounts, storing state in local browser session
Keyboard shortcuts
Export of the site's data available to give to your agent to easily create your own version
This takes ~2 hours now. I can breathe again. Thank you Opus 5.5 <3.
EDIT: A little bit more on my process. I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac). I use Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I don't actually do anything resembling traditional engineering anymore (read/write code, run commands in a terminal, or etc.), I only talk to Claude and have it do everything. In this case, the only "manual work" I did was: 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box and 3) I bought the domain name. I worked on this in between Claude's actual work so it still feels a little bit like team work :) Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, deploy, secure, harden and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

title: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical
content:
An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical
When a seven-eared stem emerged from the ground, it seemed like a miracle. What Claudio Grossi had unearthed was an ancient grain that proved to be an answer to some modern problems
Lina Zeldovich
Photographs by Clara Vannucci
November 2026
Share
Add as preferred source
At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci
Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. 
To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Even the kernels themselves were bigger than those of average wheat. And unlike the typical pale-yellow wheat kernels, they came in a rainbow of colors—yellow, black, red, white and even green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a grain farmer his whole life, had never seen anything like it. “I thought it was a freak of nature,” he says. He couldn’t find a mention of it in agricultural books.
Ears grown from the very first seeds Grossi discovered in his attic. Grossi prizes these first grains, now preserved under glass in his kitchen. Clara Vannucci
